LECTURE 0 Foundation

Your AI Development Environment

From passive reader to builder — set up everything you need to create LLMs and ship AI products
35 min read Setup & Configuration All Levels

Part 1: The Two Learning Modes

This course gives you two environments to learn in. Understanding the difference is essential before you write a single line of code.

Mode A: Browser Sandbox (Pyodide)

Every lecture includes interactive code blocks that run directly in your browser using Pyodide, a port of CPython compiled to WebAssembly. No installation needed — click Run and code executes instantly.

Can do: pure Python, NumPy, algorithm prototyping, math demos. Perfect for understanding concepts: how attention scores work, how tokenization splits text, how gradients flow.

Cannot do: access a GPU, run PyTorch or TensorFlow, load billion-parameter models, or train anything meaningful. The sandbox is a teaching tool, not a production environment.

Mode B: Real Environment (Local or Cloud)

Real LLM work requires GPUs, PyTorch with CUDA, and disk space for multi-gigabyte weights. This is where you will:

  • Train a GPT model from scratch on a real corpus
  • Fine-tune open-source models like LLaMA and Mistral
  • Deploy inference servers that respond in milliseconds
  • Build and ship 5 SaaS products
Analogy — Flight Simulator vs. Cockpit

The browser sandbox is a flight simulator: learn instruments, practice procedures, build intuition — all without leaving the ground. But to actually fly, you need a real cockpit. This course teaches in the simulator first, then puts you in the cockpit with confidence.

Let us verify your browser sandbox is working:

Part 3b: Local Deployment Guide

Running NeuralForge locally on your own machine gives you the fastest possible feedback loop and complete independence from internet connectivity. This section covers exactly what you need and how to set it up.

Minimum Hardware Requirements

Before you begin, verify your machine meets these requirements:

ComponentMinimumRecommendedNotes
RAM8 GB16 GBThe model weights and training data must fit in memory. With 8 GB you can run inference but training larger configurations may trigger swapping.
CPUModern multi-core (4+ cores)8+ cores, AVX2 supportTraining is CPU-bound when no GPU is present. More cores reduce training time roughly linearly.
Disk10 GB free20 GB freeApproximately 5 GB for the course repository and datasets, 2 GB for Python and dependencies, and the rest for model checkpoints and weights.
GPUNot requiredAny CUDA-capable GPUA GPU accelerates training dramatically but is not mandatory. The Mini GPT-2 is designed to train on CPU in reasonable time.

Step-by-Step Local Installation

Follow these steps exactly. Each command should be run in your terminal (Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on macOS/Linux).

Step 1: Clone the Repository

git clone https://github.com/add-academy/neuralforge.git
cd neuralforge

This downloads the entire course project to your computer. If you do not have Git installed, download it from git-scm.com first.

Step 2: Create a Python Virtual Environment

python -m venv venv
# On macOS/Linux:
source venv/bin/activate
# On Windows:
venv\Scripts\activate

A virtual environment isolates the project dependencies from your system Python. You will see (venv) appear in your terminal prompt when it is active.

Step 3: Install Dependencies

pip install -r requirements.txt

This installs PyTorch, FastAPI, and all other required packages. The download is approximately 1.5–2 GB depending on your platform. On a slow connection, this may take 10–15 minutes.

Running NeuralForge Locally

Once installation is complete, start the application:

python -m app

This launches the FastAPI server on http://localhost:8000. Open your browser and navigate to that address to access the NeuralForge interface. The interactive API documentation is available at http://localhost:8000/docs.

Offline Mode Considerations

NeuralForge is designed to work fully offline once installed. However, keep these points in mind:

  • First run: Some models may download pre-trained weights on first launch. Run the application once with internet access before going offline.
  • API providers: If you configure an external AI provider (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude), those calls require internet. Use AI_PROVIDER=own in your .env file for fully offline operation.
  • Package updates: You cannot install new Python packages offline. Make sure pip install -r requirements.txt completes before disconnecting.
  • Dataset downloads: Course datasets are included in the repository. No additional downloads are needed for the exercises.

Performance Expectations by Hardware Tier

Hardware TierInference SpeedTraining (1 Epoch)Experience
Entry (8 GB RAM, 4-core CPU)2–5 seconds per response15–30 minutesFunctional but slower. Close other applications to free memory.
Mid-Range (16 GB RAM, 8-core CPU)0.5–2 seconds per response5–15 minutesComfortable for all course exercises. The recommended setup.
High-End (32 GB RAM, GPU)Near-instant1–3 minutesExcellent. Training feels interactive. Experiment freely with larger configurations.
Tip: If training feels slow on your hardware, reduce the batch size in the training configuration. A smaller batch size uses less memory and can sometimes train faster on CPU, though it may require more epochs to converge.

Part 6: Your First Real PyTorch Program

Since the browser cannot run PyTorch, we will implement the same operation in both NumPy and PyTorch side by side. This is the core of every neural network: a matrix multiplication followed by a nonlinear activation — what happens in every layer of every LLM.

Python — NumPy vs PyTorch: The Same Computation 

import numpy as np, time

print("SANDBOX VERSION (NumPy on CPU)")
print("=" * 50)

np.random.seed(42)
batch, dim_in, dim_out = 4, 8, 6

X = np.random.randn(batch, dim_in).astype(np.float32) # input
W = np.random.randn(dim_in, dim_out).astype(np.float32) # weights
b = np.random.randn(dim_out).astype(np.float32) # bias

# Forward pass: Y = ReLU(X @ W + b)
Y = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)

print(f"Input: {X.shape} Weight: {W.shape}")
print(f"Output: {Y.shape} Params: {W.size + b.size}")
print(f"First row: {Y[0].round(3)}")

# Benchmark
t = time.time()
for _ in range(10000): _ = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)
print(f"\
10,000 forward passes: {time.time()-t:.3f}s (CPU)")

print("\
REAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")
print("-" * 50)
print(" import torch")
print(" X = torch.randn(4, 8, device='cuda')")
print(" W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")
print(" b = torch.randn(6, device='cuda')")
print(" Y = torch.relu(X @ W + b) # runs on GPU!")

# Why GPUs matter
print("\
WHY GPUs MATTER:")
for n in [64, 256, 1024]:
 A = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 B = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 t = time.time()
 for _ in range(100): _ = A @ B
 cpu_ms = (time.time()-t)/100*1000
 print(f" {n}x{n} matmul: CPU {cpu_ms:.2f}ms | GPU ~{max(0.01,cpu_ms/50):.2f}ms")
Key Takeaway

NumPy and PyTorch do the same math. The difference is where: CPU vs. GPU. At LLM scale (4096x4096 matrices), the GPU is 50–100x faster. That speed gap is the entire reason we need GPUs.

Part 7: Course Roadmap — What You Will Build

This course has 6 stages plus a GenAI bonus. Each ends with working code, a tested notebook, and a saved checkpoint.

Stage 1 — Foundations (Lectures 1–6)

Vectors, matrices, gradients, backpropagation. You implement a neural network from raw NumPy.

Code: backprop engine, neural net from scratch  |  Deliverable: notebooks/stage1_foundations.ipynb

Stage 2 — Tokenization & Data (Lectures 7–12)

Build a BPE tokenizer from scratch. Create data pipelines for feeding text to models.

Code: BPE tokenizer, data loader  |  Deliverable: notebooks/stage2_tokenization.ipynb

Stage 3 — Embeddings & Attention (Lectures 13–18)

Word embeddings, positional encodings, multi-head self-attention — the heart of the Transformer.

Code: src/model/attention.py  |  Deliverable: attention module with causal masking

Stage 4 — Transformer & GPT (Lectures 19–24)

Assemble attention + FFN + LayerNorm into a complete GPT model. Understand every parameter.

Code: src/model/transformer.py, src/model/gpt.py  |  Deliverable: full GPT architecture

Stage 5 — Pretraining (Lectures 25–32)

Train your GPT on real data. Mixed precision, gradient accumulation, checkpointing.

Code: src/training/trainer.py, data.py, config.py  |  Deliverable: pretrained checkpoint

Stage 6 — Fine-tuning & Alignment (Lectures 33–43)

LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning, RLHF, inference server deployment. Your model follows instructions.

Code: src/inference/generate.py, server.py  |  Deliverable: LoRA adapters + FastAPI server

GenAI Bonus — 5 SaaS Products (GenAI-1 to GenAI-5)

Build and deploy five real AI products, each with frontend, backend, and production API.

Products: Writing Assistant, Code Reviewer, RAG Chatbot, Content Moderator, Translation API

Deliverable: Each deployed with Docker, accessible via public URL

The Completeness Promise

Every stage ends with three deliverables:

  1. A Colab notebook that runs end-to-end (free GPU)
  2. Local code committed to your llm-from-scratch repository
  3. A checkpoint or artifact — saved weights, trained model, or deployed API

Complete all stages and you have a GitHub repo proving you can build LLMs from scratch, fine-tune open-source models, and ship production AI products. That is not a certificate — that is proof.

Ayto ksekina ton FastAPI server sto http://localhost:8000. Anoikse ton browser sou kai ploigisou se ayti ti diefthinsi gia na prospelasei ti diepafi tou NeuralForge. I diaderastiki tekmiriosi API einai diathesimi sto http://localhost:8000/docs.

Skepseis gia ti Leitourgia Offline

To NeuralForge einai sxediasmeno na leitourgei pliros offline molis egkatastatei. Omos, kratise ayto kata nou:

  • Proti ekteleisi: Merika montela borei na katevazoun proekpaidevmena vari stin proti ekkinisei. Trexe tin efarmogi mia fora me prosvasi sto internet prin pais offline.
  • Paroxoi API: An rythmiseis enan eksoterika paroxi AI (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude), aytes oi kliseis apailtoun internet. Xrisimopoiise AI_PROVIDER=own sto arxeio .env gia pliros offline leitourgia.
  • Enimerosis paketwn: Den boreis na egkatastisei nea paketa Python offline. Vevaiwsou oti to pip install -r requirements.txt oloklironete prin aposyndeseis.
  • Lipseis datasets: Ta datasets tou mathimatos perilamvanontai sto repository. Den apailtountai epitithemenes lipseis gia ta askiseis.

REAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")

print(" W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")

WHY GPUs MATTER:")

Teil 1: Die zwei Lernmodi

Dieser Kurs bietet dir zwei Umgebungen zum Lernen. Den Unterschied zu verstehen ist unerlässlich, bevor du auch nur eine Zeile Code schreibst.

Modus A: Browser-Sandbox (Pyodide)

Jede Lektion enthält interaktive Codeblöcke, die direkt in deinem Browser mit Pyodide laufen, einer nach WebAssembly kompilierten Portierung von CPython. Keine Installation nötig — klicke auf Run und der Code wird sofort ausgeführt.

Kann: reines Python, NumPy, Algorithmus-Prototyping, mathematische Demos. Perfekt, um Konzepte zu verstehen: wie Attention-Scores funktionieren, wie Tokenisierung Text aufteilt, wie Gradienten fließen.

Kann nicht: auf eine GPU zugreifen, PyTorch oder TensorFlow ausführen, Modelle mit Milliarden Parametern laden oder irgendetwas Nennenswertes trainieren. Die Sandbox ist ein Lehrmittel, keine Produktionsumgebung.

Modus B: Echte Umgebung (lokal oder Cloud)

Echte LLM-Arbeit erfordert GPUs, PyTorch mit CUDA und Speicherplatz für mehrere Gigabyte große Gewichte. Hier wirst du:

  • Ein GPT-Modell von Grund auf mit einem echten Korpus trainieren
  • Open-Source-Modelle wie LLaMA und Mistral fine-tunen
  • Inferenzserver bereitstellen, die in Millisekunden antworten
  • 5 SaaS-Produkte bauen und ausliefern

Die Browser-Sandbox ist ein Flugsimulator: Du lernst die Instrumente kennen, übst Abläufe, entwickelst ein Gefühl dafür — alles, ohne den Boden zu verlassen. Aber um wirklich zu fliegen, brauchst du ein echtes Cockpit. Dieser Kurs unterrichtet zuerst im Simulator und setzt dich dann mit Zuversicht ins Cockpit.

Überlegungen zum Offline-Modus

NeuralForge ist so konzipiert, dass es nach der Installation vollständig offline funktioniert. Beachte dabei jedoch Folgendes:

  • Erster Start: Manche Modelle laden beim ersten Start vortrainierte Gewichte herunter. Führe die Anwendung einmal mit Internetzugang aus, bevor du offline gehst.
  • API-Anbieter: Wenn du einen externen KI-Anbieter konfigurierst (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude), benötigen diese Aufrufe eine Internetverbindung. Verwende AI_PROVIDER=own in deiner .env-Datei für einen vollständig offline funktionierenden Betrieb.
  • Paket-Updates: Du kannst offline keine neuen Python-Pakete installieren. Stelle sicher, dass pip install -r requirements.txt abgeschlossen ist, bevor du die Verbindung trennst.
  • Datensatz-Downloads: Die Kursdatensätze sind im Repository enthalten. Für die Übungen sind keine zusätzlichen Downloads erforderlich.

Teil 6: Dein erstes echtes PyTorch-Programm

Da der Browser kein PyTorch ausführen kann, implementieren wir dieselbe Operation sowohl in NumPy als auch in PyTorch nebeneinander. Das ist der Kern jedes neuronalen Netzes: eine Matrixmultiplikation gefolgt von einer nichtlinearen Aktivierung — das, was in jeder Schicht jedes LLM passiert.

Python — NumPy vs. PyTorch: Dieselbe Berechnung 

import numpy as np, time

print("SANDBOX VERSION (NumPy on CPU)")
print("=" * 50)

np.random.seed(42)
batch, dim_in, dim_out = 4, 8, 6

X = np.random.randn(batch, dim_in).astype(np.float32) # input
W = np.random.randn(dim_in, dim_out).astype(np.float32) # weights
b = np.random.randn(dim_out).astype(np.float32) # bias

# Forward pass: Y = ReLU(X @ W + b)
Y = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)

print(f"Input: {X.shape} Weight: {W.shape}")
print(f"Output: {Y.shape} Params: {W.size + b.size}")
print(f"First row: {Y[0].round(3)}")

# Benchmark
t = time.time()
for _ in range(10000): _ = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)
print(f"\
10,000 forward passes: {time.time()-t:.3f}s (CPU)")

print("\
REAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")
print("-" * 50)
print(" import torch")
print(" X = torch.randn(4, 8, device='cuda')")
print(" W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")
print(" b = torch.randn(6, device='cuda')")
print(" Y = torch.relu(X @ W + b) # runs on GPU!")

# Why GPUs matter
print("\
WHY GPUs MATTER:")
for n in [64, 256, 1024]:
 A = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 B = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 t = time.time()
 for _ in range(100): _ = A @ B

Wichtigste Erkenntnis

NumPy und PyTorch führen dieselbe Mathematik aus. Der Unterschied ist wo: CPU vs. GPU. Bei LLM-Größenordnungen (4096x4096-Matrizen) ist die GPU 50–100x schneller. Diese Geschwindigkeitslücke ist der ganze Grund, warum wir GPUs brauchen.

بيئة تطوير الذكاء الاصطناعي الخاصة بك

من قارئ سلبي إلى بانٍ — جهّز كل ما تحتاجه لإنشاء نماذج LLM وإطلاق منتجات ذكاء اصطناعي

الجزء 1: نمطا التعلّم

يوفّر لك هذا الكورس بيئتين للتعلّم. فهم الفرق بينهما ضروري قبل أن تكتب أي سطر برمجي.

النمط أ: صندوق رمل في المتصفح (Pyodide)

تتضمن كل محاضرة كتل كود تفاعلية تعمل مباشرة في متصفحك باستخدام Pyodide، وهي نسخة من CPython مُصرَّفة إلى WebAssembly. لا حاجة لأي تثبيت — اضغط Run وسيُنفَّذ الكود فورًا.

يستطيع: تشغيل Python الخالص، وNumPy، ونمذجة الخوارزميات، والعروض الرياضية التوضيحية. مثالي لفهم المفاهيم: كيف تعمل درجات الانتباه (attention)، وكيف يقسّم الترميز (tokenization) النص، وكيف تتدفق التدرّجات (gradients).

لا يستطيع: الوصول إلى GPU، أو تشغيل PyTorch أو TensorFlow، أو تحميل نماذج بمليارات المعاملات، أو تدريب أي شيء ذي معنى. صندوق الرمل هو أداة تعليمية، وليس بيئة إنتاجية.

النمط ب: البيئة الحقيقية (محلية أو سحابية)

العمل الحقيقي على نماذج LLM يتطلب وحدات GPU، وPyTorch مع CUDA، ومساحة قرص لأوزان بحجم عدة غيغابايت. هنا ستقوم بما يلي:

  • تدريب نموذج GPT من الصفر على مجموعة نصوص حقيقية
  • ضبط دقيق (fine-tuning) لنماذج مفتوحة المصدر مثل LLaMA وMistral
  • نشر خوادم استدلال (inference) تستجيب خلال أجزاء من الثانية
  • بناء وإطلاق 5 منتجات SaaS
تشبيه — محاكي طيران مقابل قمرة قيادة

صندوق الرمل في المتصفح هو محاكي طيران: تتعلم فيه الأدوات، وتتمرّن على الإجراءات، وتبني حدسك — كل ذلك دون مغادرة الأرض. لكن للطيران فعليًا، تحتاج إلى قمرة قيادة حقيقية. يُدرِّس هذا الكورس أولًا في المحاكي، ثم يضعك في قمرة القيادة بثقة.

اعتبارات وضع العمل دون اتصال

صُمِّم NeuralForge للعمل بشكل كامل دون اتصال بالإنترنت بعد التثبيت. مع ذلك، ضع هذه النقاط في اعتبارك:

  • التشغيل الأول: قد تُنزِّل بعض النماذج أوزانًا مُدرَّبة مسبقًا عند أول تشغيل. شغّل التطبيق مرة واحدة مع اتصال بالإنترنت قبل العمل دون اتصال.
  • مزوّدو API: إذا هيّأت مزوّد ذكاء اصطناعي خارجي (OpenAI، Gemini، Claude)، فإن تلك الاستدعاءات تتطلب اتصالًا بالإنترنت. استخدم AI_PROVIDER=own في ملف .env للعمل بشكل كامل دون اتصال.
  • تحديثات الحزم: لا يمكنك تثبيت حزم Python جديدة دون اتصال. تأكد من اكتمال pip install -r requirements.txt قبل قطع الاتصال.
  • تنزيل مجموعات البيانات: مجموعات بيانات الكورس مضمّنة في المستودع. لا حاجة لأي تنزيلات إضافية للتمارين.

Python — NumPy vs PyTorch: lo stesso calcolo

print("=" * 50)

b = np.random.randn(dim_out).astype(np.float32) # bias

# Forward pass: Y = ReLU(X @ W + b)

print(f"Output: {Y.shape} Params: {W.size + b.size}")

REAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")
print("-" * 50)
print(" import torch")

print(" W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")
print(" b = torch.randn(6, device='cuda')")
print(" Y = torch.relu(X @ W + b) # runs on GPU!")

# Why GPUs matter

WHY GPUs MATTER:")
for n in [64, 256, 1024]:
 A = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 B = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)

NumPy e PyTorch eseguono la stessa matematica. La differenza è dove: CPU vs. GPU. Alla scala degli LLM (matrici 4096x4096), la GPU è 50–100 volte più veloce. Questo divario di velocità è l'intera ragione per cui abbiamo bisogno delle GPU.

Vettori, matrici, gradienti, backpropagation. Implementi una rete neurale partendo da NumPy puro.

Codice: motore di backpropagation, rete neurale da zero  |  Consegna: notebooks/stage1_foundations.ipynb

Fase 2 — Tokenizzazione e dati (Lezioni 7–12)

Costruisci un tokenizer BPE da zero. Crea pipeline di dati per fornire testo ai modelli.

Codice: tokenizer BPE, data loader  |  Consegna: notebooks/stage2_tokenization.ipynb

Fase 3 — Embedding e attenzione (Lezioni 13–18)

Word embedding, codifiche posizionali, self-attention multi-head — il cuore del Transformer.

Codice: src/model/attention.py  |  Consegna: modulo di attenzione con causal masking

Fase 4 — Transformer e GPT (Lezioni 19–24)

Assembla attenzione + FFN + LayerNorm in un modello GPT completo. Comprendi ogni parametro.

Codice: src/model/transformer.py, src/model/gpt.py  |  Consegna: architettura GPT completa

Fase 5 — Pretraining (Lezioni 25–32)

Addestra il tuo GPT su dati reali. Precisione mista, accumulo dei gradienti, checkpointing.

Codice: src/training/trainer.py, data.py, config.py  |  Consegna: checkpoint pre-addestrato

Fase 6 — Fine-tuning e allineamento (Lezioni 33–43)

Fine-tuning LoRA/QLoRA, RLHF, distribuzione del server di inferenza. Il tuo modello segue le istruzioni.

Codice: src/inference/generate.py, server.py  |  Consegna: adattatori LoRA + server FastAPI

Bonus GenAI — 5 prodotti SaaS (GenAI-1 – GenAI-5)

Costruisci e distribuisci cinque prodotti AI reali, ciascuno con frontend, backend e API di produzione.

Prodotti: Assistente di scrittura, Revisore di codice, Chatbot RAG, Moderatore di contenuti, API di traduzione

Consegna: Ognuno distribuito con Docker, accessibile tramite URL pubblico

Ogni fase termina con tre consegne:

  1. Un notebook Colab che funziona end-to-end (GPU gratuita)

Partie 1 : les deux modes d'apprentissage

Ce cours vous propose deux environnements pour apprendre. Comprendre la différence est essentiel avant d'écrire la moindre ligne de code.

Mode A : bac à sable dans le navigateur (Pyodide)

Chaque cours comprend des blocs de code interactifs qui s'exécutent directement dans votre navigateur grâce à Pyodide, un portage de CPython compilé en WebAssembly. Aucune installation n'est nécessaire — cliquez sur Run et le code s'exécute instantanément.

Ce qu'il peut faire : Python pur, NumPy, prototypage d'algorithmes, démonstrations mathématiques. Parfait pour comprendre les concepts : comment fonctionnent les scores d'attention, comment la tokenisation découpe le texte, comment circulent les gradients.

Ce qu'il ne peut pas faire : accéder à un GPU, exécuter PyTorch ou TensorFlow, charger des modèles à des milliards de paramètres, ou entraîner quoi que ce soit de significatif. Le bac à sable est un outil pédagogique, pas un environnement de production.

Mode B : environnement réel (local ou cloud)

Le vrai travail sur les LLM nécessite des GPU, PyTorch avec CUDA, et de l'espace disque pour des poids de plusieurs gigaoctets. C'est ici que vous allez :

  • Entraîner un modèle GPT à partir de zéro sur un vrai corpus
  • Affiner (fine-tuner) des modèles open source comme LLaMA et Mistral
  • Déployer des serveurs d'inférence qui répondent en quelques millisecondes
  • Construire et livrer 5 produits SaaS
Analogie — simulateur de vol vs. cockpit

Le bac à sable du navigateur est un simulateur de vol : apprenez les instruments, entraînez-vous aux procédures, développez votre intuition — sans jamais quitter le sol. Mais pour voler réellement, il vous faut un vrai cockpit. Ce cours enseigne d'abord dans le simulateur, puis vous installe dans le cockpit en toute confiance.

NeuralForge est conçu pour fonctionner entièrement hors ligne une fois installé. Toutefois, gardez ces points à l'esprit :

  • Fournisseurs d'API : si vous configurez un fournisseur d'IA externe (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude), ces appels nécessitent internet. Utilisez AI_PROVIDER=own dans votre fichier .env pour un fonctionnement entièrement hors ligne.

  • Téléchargement des jeux de données : les jeux de données du cours sont inclus dans le dépôt. Aucun téléchargement supplémentaire n'est nécessaire pour les exercices.

Partie 6 : votre premier vrai programme PyTorch

Comme le navigateur ne peut pas exécuter PyTorch, nous allons implémenter la même opération à la fois en NumPy et en PyTorch, côte à côte. C'est le cœur de tout réseau de neurones : une multiplication de matrices suivie d'une activation non linéaire — ce qui se passe dans chaque couche de chaque LLM.

Python — NumPy vs PyTorch : le même calcul 

import numpy as np, time

print("SANDBOX VERSION (NumPy on CPU)")
print("=" * 50)

np.random.seed(42)
batch, dim_in, dim_out = 4, 8, 6

X = np.random.randn(batch, dim_in).astype(np.float32) # input
W = np.random.randn(dim_in, dim_out).astype(np.float32) # weights
b = np.random.randn(dim_out).astype(np.float32) # bias

# Forward pass: Y = ReLU(X @ W + b)
Y = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)

print(f"Input: {X.shape} Weight: {W.shape}")
print(f"Output: {Y.shape} Params: {W.size + b.size}")
print(f"First row: {Y[0].round(3)}")

# Benchmark
t = time.time()
for _ in range(10000): _ = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)
print(f"\
10,000 forward passes: {time.time()-t:.3f}s (CPU)")

print("\
REAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")
print("-" * 50)
print(" import torch")
print(" X = torch.randn(4, 8, device='cuda')")
print(" W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")
print(" b = torch.randn(6, device='cuda')")
print(" Y = torch.relu(X @ W + b) # runs on GPU!")

# Why GPUs matter
print("\
WHY GPUs MATTER:")
for n in [64, 256, 1024]:
 A = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 B = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
 t = time.time()
 for _ in range(100): _ = A @ B
 cpu_ms = (time.time()-t)/100*1000
 print(f" {n}x{n} matmul: CPU {cpu_ms:.2f}ms | GPU ~{max(0.01,cpu_ms/50):.2f}ms")
Point clé à retenir

NumPy et PyTorch effectuent les mêmes calculs. La différence est l'endroit où ils s'exécutent : CPU vs. GPU. À l'échelle des LLM (matrices 4096x4096), le GPU est 50–100 fois plus rapide. Cet écart de vitesse est toute la raison pour laquelle nous avons besoin de GPU.

import numpy as np, time

print("SANDBOX VERSION (NumPy on CPU)")
print("=" * 50)

np.random.seed(42)
batch, dim_in, dim_out = 4, 8, 6

X = np.random.randn(batch, dim_in).astype(np.float32)   # input
W = np.random.randn(dim_in, dim_out).astype(np.float32) # weights
b = np.random.randn(dim_out).astype(np.float32)          # bias

# Forward pass: Y = ReLU(X @ W + b)
Y = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)

print(f"Input:  {X.shape}   Weight: {W.shape}")
print(f"Output: {Y.shape}   Params: {W.size + b.size}")
print(f"First row: {Y[0].round(3)}")

# Benchmark
t = time.time()
for _ in range(10000): _ = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)
print(f"\n10,000 forward passes: {time.time()-t:.3f}s (CPU)")

print("\nREAL VERSION (paste on your machine):")
print("-" * 50)
print("  import torch")
print("  X = torch.randn(4, 8, device='cuda')")
print("  W = torch.randn(8, 6, device='cuda')")
print("  b = torch.randn(6, device='cuda')")
print("  Y = torch.relu(X @ W + b)  # runs on GPU!")

# Why GPUs matter
print("\nWHY GPUs MATTER:")
for n in [64, 256, 1024]:
    A = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
    B = np.random.randn(n, n).astype(np.float32)
    t = time.time()
    for _ in range(100): _ = A @ B
    cpu_ms = (time.time()-t)/100*1000
    print(f"  {n}x{n} matmul: CPU {cpu_ms:.2f}ms | GPU ~{max(0.01,cpu_ms/50):.2f}ms")
